extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians (especially newer/developing performers) seeking advice on club bookings and fee negotiation
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for comedians on how to respond when a club booker asks about your fee, how to gather leverage/information, how to calculate costs, and how to decide whether to accept a booking. Focused on club weekends and first-time bookings but notes other markets (corporate/cruise/college).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify number of shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with this: "How many shows are you looking for me to do?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five shows over a weekend is very different from one showcase appearance. Confirming how many shows (and the format) affects total fee and whether a quoted price is reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask what they usually pay first-timers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask: "What do you usually pay your first-time headliners, features, or openers?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fair, professional question that lets the booker reveal their typical rate structure instead of forcing you to guess. It helps you avoid lowballing yourself and shows you're informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do your market research / find out going rates
rubrics_metrics.description: You should also do some research. If you know comedians who have worked the club — and you’re on good enough terms to ask — find out what the club typically pays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians don’t have a union; information is often the only leverage performers have. Use peers and past bookings to estimate typical pay for openers, features, and headliners in that city/venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect boundaries when asking peers about pay
rubrics_metrics.description: Be respectful. Some entertainers are private about money, and that’s understandable too. Don’t push if someone seems uncomfortable discussing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek information but avoid pressuring colleagues; preserve relationships and professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the booker show their cards first
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask what they’re offering first. Let the booker show his cards before you show yours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid immediately throwing out a random number. If you name a price too quickly you may undercut your value; let the booker state an initial offer so you can negotiate from information, not insecurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid underselling yourself to get the booking
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s always the chance you’ll come in low just to get the booking. That’s especially common with newer comedians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t quote too low just to 'get in the door' with the expectation of renegotiating later; this can lock you into lower pay and set poor precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate your trip/projected expenses before accepting
rubrics_metrics.description: You absolutely need to calculate your expenses before agreeing to anything. Know what the trip will realistically cost you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include airfare (if applicable), hotel, transportation, meals, and other out-of-pocket costs. Compare your total cost against the club's offer to determine if the deal is worth it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for travel/housing savings (e.g., staying with family)
rubrics_metrics.description: In your case, staying with your grandmother could actually become part of the negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you’re saving on hotel or transport (staying with family, borrowing a car), mention it — it may reduce the fee you need or be offered as a negotiating point (e.g., the club might not provide a hotel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm which expenses the club covers
rubrics_metrics.description: A lot of clubs no longer cover airfare the way they once did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask explicitly whether the club will cover airfare, hotel, ground transportation, and meals so you can factor covered/uncovered costs into your decision and negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider non-monetary value (credits, networking, market exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself: Is this a strong credit for my resume? Will I meet people who could help me get more work? Is this an opportunity to expand into a new market? Would I enjoy the trip personally?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh intangible benefits against pay — sometimes lower pay is acceptable if the gig advances your career, provides key contacts, or opens a new market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand market leverage based on credits and drawing power
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics with major credits, television exposure, and audience-drawing power can often name their price. Newer comics usually can’t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize your position: established performers set their price; developing comedians should focus on information-gathering and building credits to increase leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize differences across booking markets
rubrics_metrics.description: You’ll hear this same approach in the corporate, cruise, and college markets too. The difference is that established comedians in those worlds usually already have a set fee structure and know how to negotiate travel, hotel, meals, merchandise percentages, and other expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Club work varies widely by venue, city, audience size, and drawing power; corporate/cruise/college bookings often have clearer fee structures and negotiable rider items (travel, hotel, meals, merch splits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate specific contract items (travel, hotel, meals, merch percentage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Established comedians ... know how to negotiate travel, hotel, meals, merchandise percentages, and other expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you have leverage, explicitly negotiate those line items rather than treating pay as a single number. Clarify percentages, per diems, and who pays for what.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate from information, not insecurity; stay professional and honest
rubrics_metrics.description: My advice is to stay professional, be honest, and avoid throwing out a random number too quickly. ... Then negotiate from a position of information — not insecurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain professionalism in communication, be transparent about constraints (e.g., expenses, availability), and use gathered information to make a reasoned counteroffer rather than reacting emotionally.
